To: Renters Board / Notices
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: URGENT – stop using Brightline Pro 6% (20 vol) 1L, batch LX2291

Hiya everyone,

Please read this before doing any bleach or colour work. Kelvin Trade has issued a product notice saying a filling error has affected Brightline Pro 6% (20 vol) Cream Developer 1L, batch LX2291. Bottles labelled 6% may actually contain 12% (40 vol) developer – double the strength shown on the bottle.

Kelvin says this batch was supplied between 19 October and 5 November 2026. Other batches and strengths are not affected, according to the supplier.

This is a safety issue, not just an inconvenience. A client here has had a scalp burn following a service where a bottle from this batch was used. Another renter using the same batch had exceptionally fast lift and very hot foils. At least two renters have confirmed they had LX2291, and others may have bought from the same rep.

HOW TO CHECK YOUR BOTTLES

Check the base of every bottle for batch code LX2291.

Do not just check the box – the batch code is not shown on the box. It is printed on the base of the bottle itself.

Check:
• Open and part-used bottles on your trolley or at your station.
• Bottles in cupboards and stock in the back.
• Unopened bottles and any still in boxes.
• Anything bought from the Kelvin Trade rep during the supply dates above.

A bottle being new, unopened or previously used without an obvious problem does not make it safe. The only way to identify this affected batch is to check the code on the bottle base.

WHAT TO DO WITH THEM

Stop using LX2291 immediately. Separate the bottles from your working stock and mark them clearly so nobody picks one up by mistake.

The Kelvin rep is due in on Tuesday 10 November. Affected bottles can be handed back to him or taken to Kelvin Trade’s Hillington depot for a full credit.

IMPORTANT: if you have had a reaction, an abnormal service or another problem with a bottle, keep that bottle back as evidence. Do not bin it or hand it back. Store it safely away from use, photograph the batch code and keep your notes and any other relevant records.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR

Because the developer may be twice the labelled strength, processing can be much faster than expected. Possible warning signs include unusually rapid lift, foils becoming very hot, strong burning rather than mild tingling, scalp redness or soreness, and patchy or brassy colour results.

Over-processing can also leave hair dry, damaged, weak or at risk of breakage. These signs do not prove a bottle is from the affected batch, but stop the service and check the bottle rather than assuming the heat or speed is normal. Do not encourage a client to put up with burning.

IF SOMEBODY REACTS IN THE CHAIR

Stop the service immediately. Protect yourself with gloves and carefully remove contaminated clothing if possible.

Rinse the affected area with plenty of cool or lukewarm running water for about one hour. Do not use shampoo, and do not apply creams or other chemicals, including soothing products.

For a suspected chemical burn, call 999 for medical help immediately. Do not wait for blistering or severe pain. Chemical burns need hospital assessment. Follow the call handler’s instructions.

Call 999 immediately for breathing difficulty, throat swelling or collapse as well.

Once urgent care is underway, record what happened in the incident book at the desk, including the product, batch code, timings and symptoms.

NHS guidance: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/acid-and-chemical-burns/

Please check your trolley and your back stock today, before another bottle gets used.

Cheers,
Kirsty
